```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(readr); library(stringr)
library(glmnet); library(lmtest); library(sandwich); library(ggrepel); library(scales); library(knitr)
set.seed(123)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

# 1. Data and checks

**Unit of analysis.** The source file holds *quarterly snapshots* (March, June, September, December) of ODSP cases for 15 Ontario CMAs. I aggregate to CMA-year. `total_cases` is therefore the sum of four quarterly snapshots (a caseload *index*, not a count of unique people). 2025 has only two quarters and is dropped.

**Average duration.** Each case is in one of three duration buckets. I assign each bucket a typical value (0–35 months → 17.5, 36–59 → 47.5, 60+ → 72) and take the case-weighted mean. The 60+ bucket is open-ended, so 72 is an assumption; the sensitivity check below tests it.

```{r load}
raw <- read_csv("D:/ODSP_Project/ODSP_CMA.csv", show_col_types = FALSE, name_repair = "minimal")
raw <- raw[, names(raw) != ""]                          # drop unnamed empty column
n_raw <- nrow(raw)
raw <- raw %>% filter(rowSums(is.na(.)) < ncol(.))       # drop fully blank rows
cat("Rows in file:", n_raw, "| fully blank rows removed:", n_raw - nrow(raw), "| rows kept:", nrow(raw), "\n")

odsp_clean <- raw %>%
  rename(snapshot = Month, cma_code = `CMA Code`, cma_name = CMA, total_cases = Cases,
         single = FTS, single_parent = FTSP, couple = FTC,
         family_size_1 = FS1, family_size_2 = FS2, family_size_3_plus = FS3,
         age_24_or_less = Age24, age_25_to_54 = Age2554, age_55_plus = Age55,
         male_applicant = Male, female_applicant = Female,
         months_0_35 = Moa035, months_36_59 = Moa3659, months_60_plus = Moa60) %>%
  mutate(cma_name = str_trim(gsub("--", "-", str_remove(cma_name, "^[0-9]+\\s?-\\s?"))),
         year = floor(snapshot / 100)) %>%
  filter(year < 2025)

# Every CMA-year must have exactly 4 quarterly snapshots
stopifnot(all(count(odsp_clean, year, cma_name)$n == 4))
```

```{r annual}
sum_cols <- c("total_cases","single","single_parent","couple","family_size_1","family_size_2",
              "family_size_3_plus","age_24_or_less","age_25_to_54","age_55_plus",
              "male_applicant","female_applicant","months_0_35","months_36_59","months_60_plus")

make_annual <- function(d, v_short = 17.5, v_mid = 47.5, v_long = 72) {
  d %>% group_by(year, cma_code, cma_name) %>%
    summarise(across(all_of(sum_cols), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(avg_months = (months_0_35*v_short + months_36_59*v_mid + months_60_plus*v_long) / total_cases,
           prop_single = single/total_cases, prop_single_parent = single_parent/total_cases,
           prop_couple = couple/total_cases, prop_age_24_or_less = age_24_or_less/total_cases,
           prop_age_25_to_54 = age_25_to_54/total_cases, prop_age_55_plus = age_55_plus/total_cases,
           prop_male = male_applicant/total_cases, prop_female = female_applicant/total_cases,
           prop_fs1 = family_size_1/total_cases, prop_fs3_plus = family_size_3_plus/total_cases)
}
odsp_annual <- make_annual(odsp_clean)

# Validity checks: each set of categories should add up to total cases
chk <- odsp_annual %>% summarise(
  household = max(abs(single + single_parent + couple - total_cases)),
  age       = max(abs(age_24_or_less + age_25_to_54 + age_55_plus - total_cases)),
  duration  = max(abs(months_0_35 + months_36_59 + months_60_plus - total_cases)),
  family    = max(abs(family_size_1 + family_size_2 + family_size_3_plus - total_cases)),
  gender    = max(abs(male_applicant + female_applicant - total_cases)))
kable(chk, caption = "Largest absolute gap (cases) between category sums and total, across all CMA-years")
stopifnot(chk$household == 0, chk$age == 0, chk$duration == 0, chk$family == 0)
cat("Single-adult and family-size-1 are identical in every row:",
    all(odsp_annual$family_size_1 == odsp_annual$single), "\n")
```

Household, age, duration and family-size categories add to the total exactly. Gender is off by at most a handful of cases (the check above shows the size), which is immaterial. `family_size_1` is identical to `single`, which is why one of them is dropped from the models.

## Sensitivity of the 60+ assumption

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- lapply(c(72, 84, 96), function(v)
  make_annual(odsp_clean, v_long = v) %>% group_by(cma_name) %>%
    summarise(avg = mean(avg_months), .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(v = v, rank = rank(-avg))) %>% bind_rows()
sens_w <- sens %>% select(cma_name, v, rank) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = v, values_from = rank, names_prefix = "rank_at_")
kable(sens_w %>% arrange(rank_at_72), caption = "CMA rank (1 = longest duration) if the 60+ bucket is valued at 72, 84 or 96 months")
```

Rankings barely move, so the *ordering* of CMAs is robust to this assumption. The *levels* (e.g., "58 months") are not: they depend directly on the assumed value.

# 2. How has duration changed over time? (Q1 and Q2)

```{r q1q2}
sys <- odsp_annual %>% group_by(year) %>% summarise(
  avg_duration = sum(avg_months * total_cases) / sum(total_cases),
  caseload_index = sum(total_cases),
  share_0_35 = sum(months_0_35) / sum(total_cases),
  share_60_plus = sum(months_60_plus) / sum(total_cases))

p1 <- ggplot(sys, aes(year, avg_duration)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Case-weighted average months on ODSP, all 15 CMAs", x = NULL, y = "Months (estimated)") + theme_minimal()
print(p1); ggsave("figures/q1_duration_trend.png", p1, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)

p2 <- ggplot(sys, aes(year, caseload_index)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Caseload index (sum of four quarterly snapshots)", x = NULL, y = "Index") + theme_minimal()
print(p2); ggsave("figures/q2_caseload_trend.png", p2, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)

kable(sys %>% mutate(across(starts_with("share"), ~ round(100 * .x, 1)), avg_duration = round(avg_duration, 2)) %>%
        filter(year %in% c(2003, 2010, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024)),
      caption = "Selected years: shares are % of cases")
```

What the data actually show: average duration fell from 2003 to about 2010, rose through 2016, **fell again 2017–2019**, then rose sharply 2020–2022 and flattened in 2023–2024 (slightly down in 2024). It is **not** a steady rise since 2015. Caseload peaked in 2020 and has been roughly flat-to-lower since.

The 2020–2022 rise coincides with the share of cases in the 0–35 month bucket falling and the 60+ share rising. That is consistent with **fewer recent entrants and/or longer stays**; these data cannot separate the two.

# 3. Regional segmentation (Q3)

```{r q3}
cma <- odsp_annual %>% group_by(cma_name) %>%
  summarise(avg_duration = sum(avg_months * total_cases) / sum(total_cases),
            contribution = sum(avg_months * total_cases), .groups = "drop")
med_d <- median(cma$avg_duration); med_c <- median(cma$contribution)
cma <- cma %>% mutate(
  segment = case_when(
    avg_duration >  med_d & contribution >  med_c ~ "High duration / High contribution",
    avg_duration >  med_d & contribution <= med_c ~ "High duration / Low contribution",
    avg_duration <= med_d & contribution >  med_c ~ "Low duration / High contribution",
    TRUE                                          ~ "Low duration / Low contribution"))
kable(cma %>% arrange(desc(avg_duration)) %>% mutate(contribution = round(contribution / 1e6, 1)),
      digits = 2, caption = "Contribution in millions of (case-snapshot × months). Median split on 15 CMAs.")
cat("Median duration:", round(med_d, 2), " Median contribution (M):", round(med_c / 1e6, 1), "\n")
cat("CMAs sitting exactly on a median (assigned by the <= rule):",
    paste(cma$cma_name[cma$avg_duration == med_d | cma$contribution == med_c], collapse = ", "), "\n")

p3 <- ggplot(cma, aes(avg_duration, contribution / 1e6, colour = segment, label = cma_name)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = med_d, linetype = 2) + geom_hline(yintercept = med_c / 1e6, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + geom_text_repel(size = 3, show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = 30) +
  labs(title = "CMA segments: duration vs. cumulative contribution", x = "Average months on ODSP (2003–2024)",
       y = "Contribution (millions)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(p3); ggsave("figures/q3_segmentation.png", p3, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 150)
```

**Caveats.** Segments come from a median split of 15 points, so a CMA right at a median (see the line above) can flip with a small change. Toronto's contribution is several times every other CMA's; a median split depends only on rank, so a log transform would not change the segments and I do not present one as a robustness check.

# 4. Do demographics explain regional differences? (Q4)

```{r q4}
# Simple average of the 22 annual values per CMA (each year counts equally)
cma_dem <- odsp_annual %>% group_by(cma_name) %>%
  summarise(avg_duration = mean(avg_months),
            across(c(prop_single, prop_single_parent, prop_couple, prop_age_24_or_less,
                     prop_age_25_to_54, prop_age_55_plus, prop_male, prop_fs3_plus), mean), .groups = "drop")
vars <- setdiff(names(cma_dem), c("cma_name", "avg_duration"))
cors <- sapply(vars, function(v) cor(cma_dem$avg_duration, cma_dem[[v]]))
pv   <- sapply(vars, function(v) cor.test(cma_dem$avg_duration, cma_dem[[v]])$p.value)
cor_tab <- data.frame(variable = vars, r = round(cors, 3), p_value = round(pv, 3)) %>% arrange(desc(r))
kable(cor_tab, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Correlation with average duration across 15 CMAs (9 uncorrected tests)")

p4 <- ggplot(cma_dem, aes(prop_age_25_to_54, avg_duration, label = cma_name)) +
  geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey40") + geom_text_repel(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Share aged 25–54 vs. average duration (15 CMAs)", x = "Share aged 25–54", y = "Average months") + theme_minimal()
print(p4); ggsave("figures/q4_correlation_scatter.png", p4, width = 8, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)

seg_dem <- cma_dem %>% left_join(cma %>% select(cma_name, segment), by = "cma_name") %>%
  group_by(segment) %>% summarise(across(c(prop_single, prop_single_parent, prop_couple,
        prop_age_24_or_less, prop_age_25_to_54, prop_age_55_plus), mean), .groups = "drop")
kable(seg_dem, digits = 3, caption = "Mean demographic shares by segment")

hh <- seg_dem %>% select(segment, prop_single, prop_single_parent, prop_couple) %>%
  pivot_longer(-segment, names_to = "type", values_to = "share")
p5 <- ggplot(hh, aes(segment, share, fill = type)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) + labs(title = "Household composition by segment", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme_minimal()
print(p5); ggsave("figures/q4_household_composition.png", p5, width = 9, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
ag <- seg_dem %>% select(segment, prop_age_24_or_less, prop_age_25_to_54, prop_age_55_plus) %>%
  pivot_longer(-segment, names_to = "type", values_to = "share")
p6 <- ggplot(ag, aes(segment, share, fill = type)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) + labs(title = "Age composition by segment", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme_minimal()
print(p6); ggsave("figures/q4_age_composition.png", p6, width = 9, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
```

Demographic mix is similar across segments. With 15 CMAs and nine uncorrected tests, only one correlation (25–54 share) reaches p < 0.05, and one hit in nine tests is not strong evidence. Treat the correlations as descriptive.

# 5. Modelling (Q5)

## 5.1 Setup

Target: `avg_months` in year *t*. Predictors: average duration in years *t-1*, *t-2*, *t-3* and demographic shares from year *t-1* (so nothing from year *t* leaks in). Splits are chronological: **train 2006–2019, validation 2020–2021 (tuning only), test 2022–2024 (touched once for final reporting)**.

```{r model_data}
model_df <- odsp_annual %>% arrange(cma_name, year) %>% group_by(cma_name) %>%
  mutate(lag1_avg_months = lag(avg_months, 1), lag2_avg_months = lag(avg_months, 2), lag3_avg_months = lag(avg_months, 3),
         across(c(prop_single, prop_single_parent, prop_age_24_or_less, prop_age_55_plus, prop_male, prop_fs3_plus),
                ~ lag(.x, 1), .names = "lag1_{.col}")) %>% ungroup() %>% filter(!is.na(lag3_avg_months))
dem  <- c("lag1_prop_single","lag1_prop_single_parent","lag1_prop_age_24_or_less",
          "lag1_prop_age_55_plus","lag1_prop_male","lag1_prop_fs3_plus")
lags <- c("lag1_avg_months","lag2_avg_months","lag3_avg_months")
xcols <- c(lags, dem)
train <- filter(model_df, year <= 2019); val <- filter(model_df, year %in% 2020:2021); test <- filter(model_df, year >= 2022)
c(train = nrow(train), validation = nrow(val), test = nrow(test))
rmse <- function(a, p) sqrt(mean((a - p)^2)); mae <- function(a, p) mean(abs(a - p))
```

## 5.2 Baselines: naive and linear regression

The simplest forecast is "next year equals this year". Any model must beat it.

```{r ols}
ols <- lm(avg_months ~ lag1_avg_months + lag1_prop_single + lag1_prop_single_parent + lag1_prop_age_24_or_less +
            lag1_prop_age_55_plus + lag1_prop_male + lag1_prop_fs3_plus, data = train)
cat("Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(ols)$adj.r.squared, 3), "\n")
bptest(ols); dwtest(ols)
```

Both diagnostics fail: residual variance is not constant (Breusch-Pagan p ≈ 0.01) and residuals are strongly autocorrelated within CMAs (Durbin-Watson ≈ 0.95, p < 0.001). Standard OLS errors are therefore too small. I report errors clustered by CMA (15 clusters, so still approximate; t-test with 14 df).

```{r ols_cl}
cl <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovCL(ols, cluster = train$cma_name), df = 14); cl
```

```{r ols_diag}
png("figures/lm_residual_diagnostics.png", width = 1200, height = 500, res = 130)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot(fitted(ols), resid(ols), xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual", main = "Residuals vs fitted"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(resid(ols)); qqline(resid(ols)); dev.off()
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot(fitted(ols), resid(ols), xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual", main = "Residuals vs fitted"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(resid(ols)); qqline(resid(ols)); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 5.3 Elastic Net

Elastic Net handles the correlated lags and demographics. I choose `alpha` by **validation** RMSE (not test), and within each alpha use cross-validation on train. I use `lambda.min`; the more conservative `lambda.1se` over-shrinks in this setting (compared below).

```{r en}
Xm <- function(d) as.matrix(d[, xcols])
alphas <- seq(0, 1, 0.1)
grid <- lapply(alphas, function(a) {
  cv <- cv.glmnet(Xm(train), train$avg_months, alpha = a, nfolds = 10)
  data.frame(alpha = a, val_rmse = rmse(val$avg_months, as.numeric(predict(cv, Xm(val), s = "lambda.min"))))
}) %>% bind_rows()
best_alpha <- grid$alpha[which.min(grid$val_rmse)]
kable(grid, digits = 3, caption = "Validation RMSE by alpha")
pa <- ggplot(grid, aes(alpha, val_rmse)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + geom_point(data = filter(grid, alpha == best_alpha), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Alpha selected on validation data", x = "alpha (0 = ridge, 1 = lasso)", y = "Validation RMSE") + theme_minimal()
print(pa); ggsave("figures/alpha_selection.png", pa, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
cat("Selected alpha:", best_alpha, "(a mix of ridge and lasso). Apart from pure ridge (alpha = 0), validation RMSE is within about 0.96–1.03 for every alpha, so the exact choice matters little; I still call it Elastic Net because it is not at either extreme\n")

set.seed(123)
cv_en <- cv.glmnet(Xm(train), train$avg_months, alpha = best_alpha, nfolds = 10)
```

```{r compare}
pred <- function(d, s) as.numeric(predict(cv_en, Xm(d), s = s))
perf <- bind_rows(lapply(list(Train = train, Validation = val, Test = test), function(d) data.frame(
  `Naive (last year)` = rmse(d$avg_months, d$lag1_avg_months),
  `Linear regression` = rmse(d$avg_months, predict(ols, d)),
  `Elastic Net (lambda.min)` = rmse(d$avg_months, pred(d, "lambda.min")),
  `Elastic Net (lambda.1se)` = rmse(d$avg_months, pred(d, "lambda.1se")), check.names = FALSE)), .id = "Dataset")
kable(perf, digits = 3, caption = "RMSE (months)")

test_cmp <- test %>% mutate(en = pred(test, "lambda.min")) %>% group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(`Elastic Net` = rmse(avg_months, en), Naive = rmse(avg_months, lag1_avg_months), .groups = "drop")
kable(test_cmp, digits = 3, caption = "Test RMSE by year")
```

The validation window (2020–2021) is hard for every method (the COVID period). Elastic Net beats the naive forecast in each test year, but 2022 is the only year with a large gap and the model has only three test years to be judged on.

```{r pva}
tp <- test %>% mutate(pred = pred(test, "lambda.min"))
pp <- ggplot(tp, aes(avg_months, pred, colour = factor(year))) + geom_abline(linetype = 2) + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Test set: predicted vs actual average months", x = "Actual", y = "Predicted", colour = "Year") + theme_minimal()
print(pp); ggsave("figures/predicted_vs_actual.png", pp, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 150)
```

### Uncertainty (bootstrap over CMAs)

```{r boot}
set.seed(123)
tp <- tp %>% mutate(ols_pred = predict(ols, test))
cmas <- unique(tp$cma_name)
bs <- replicate(2000, { s <- sample(cmas, replace = TRUE); d <- bind_rows(lapply(s, function(x) filter(tp, cma_name == x)))
  c(vs_lin = 1 - rmse(d$avg_months, d$pred) / rmse(d$avg_months, d$ols_pred),
    vs_naive = 1 - rmse(d$avg_months, d$pred) / rmse(d$avg_months, d$lag1_avg_months)) })
kable(round(100 * apply(bs, 1, quantile, c(.025, .5, .975)), 1), caption = "% RMSE reduction of Elastic Net, bootstrap over CMAs")
```

This interval reflects variation across regions only. It does **not** reflect uncertainty about future years and is probably too narrow with 15 clusters.

## 5.4 What drives the predictions?

Coefficients are standardized (raw coefficient × predictor SD) so predictors on different scales are comparable. None were shrunk exactly to zero.

```{r coefs}
co <- coef(cv_en, s = "lambda.min"); b <- setNames(as.numeric(co[-1]), xcols)
imp <- data.frame(variable = xcols, standardized_coef = b * apply(Xm(train), 2, sd)) %>%
  mutate(status = ifelse(abs(standardized_coef) < 1e-8, "Zeroed out", "Kept")) %>% arrange(desc(abs(standardized_coef)))
kable(imp, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
pf <- ggplot(imp, aes(reorder(variable, abs(standardized_coef)), standardized_coef)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Standardized Elastic Net coefficients", x = NULL, y = "Coefficient × SD of predictor") + theme_minimal()
print(pf); ggsave("figures/feature_importance.png", pf, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)

decomp <- c(level = unname(sum(b[lags])), last_year_change = unname(-(b[2] + b[3])), prior_year_change = unname(-b[3]))
round(decomp, 3)
```

The three lags re-express as: a **level** term (~0.9, slightly below one), a positive weight on the **most recent year-over-year change**, and a small negative weight on the change before that. That is momentum (extrapolating last year's change), not "mean reversion".

```{r lagsonly}
set.seed(123)
cv_lag <- cv.glmnet(as.matrix(train[, lags]), train$avg_months, alpha = best_alpha, nfolds = 10)
lag_only <- sapply(list(Validation = val, Test = test), function(d) rmse(d$avg_months, as.numeric(predict(cv_lag, as.matrix(d[, lags]), s = "lambda.min"))))
full <- sapply(list(Validation = val, Test = test), function(d) rmse(d$avg_months, pred(d, "lambda.min")))
kable(rbind(`Lags only` = lag_only, `Lags + demographics` = full), digits = 3, caption = "RMSE: do demographics add predictive value?")
```

Adding demographics **improves validation RMSE but worsens test RMSE**, so there is no consistent predictive gain. This is a statement about prediction, not about causes.

# 6. One-year-ahead forecast (2025)

To predict 2025, the inputs must be: lag1 = 2024, lag2 = 2023, lag3 = 2022 durations and 2024 demographic shares. The final model is refit on all usable rows (2006–2024) with the validated alpha and lambda.

```{r forecast}
all_rows <- bind_rows(train, val, test)
en_final <- glmnet(Xm(all_rows), all_rows$avg_months, alpha = best_alpha, lambda = cv_en$lambda.min)

wide <- odsp_annual %>% filter(year %in% 2022:2024) %>% select(cma_name, year, avg_months) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = avg_months, names_prefix = "y")
dem24 <- odsp_annual %>% filter(year == 2024) %>% transmute(cma_name,
  lag1_prop_single = prop_single, lag1_prop_single_parent = prop_single_parent,
  lag1_prop_age_24_or_less = prop_age_24_or_less, lag1_prop_age_55_plus = prop_age_55_plus,
  lag1_prop_male = prop_male, lag1_prop_fs3_plus = prop_fs3_plus)
fx <- wide %>% transmute(cma_name, lag1_avg_months = y2024, lag2_avg_months = y2023, lag3_avg_months = y2022, avg_2024 = y2024) %>%
  left_join(dem24, by = "cma_name")
fx$pred_2025 <- as.numeric(predict(en_final, as.matrix(fx[, xcols])))
fx <- fx %>% mutate(change = pred_2025 - avg_2024) %>% arrange(desc(pred_2025))
kable(fx %>% select(cma_name, avg_2024, pred_2025, change), digits = 2, caption = "Predicted 2025 average months (estimated scale)")

pc <- ggplot(fx, aes(reorder(cma_name, pred_2025), pred_2025)) + geom_col() + coord_flip(ylim = c(min(fx$pred_2025) - 2, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted 2025 average months on ODSP", x = NULL, y = "Months (estimated)") + theme_minimal()
print(pc); ggsave("figures/cma_risk_forecast.png", pc, width = 8, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
```

Fourteen of 15 CMAs are predicted to fall slightly, in line with the 2024 decline (14 of 15 CMAs fell that year): the model extrapolates last year's change. The top five (Kingston, Peterborough, Thunder Bay, Greater Sudbury, St. Catharines-Niagara) are separated from the rest by small margins.

**Read this as a ranking, not a level forecast.** The forecast mostly mirrors the 2024 ranking (a model with a lag coefficient near 0.9 will do that). It is a one-step-ahead extrapolation, with no accounting for policy or economic change, and says nothing about causes.

# 7. Limitations

* 15 regions and 19 usable years: small samples, strongly correlated within region.
* Duration is *estimated* from three buckets with an assumed value for the open-ended 60+ bucket; levels are assumption-dependent, rankings are not.
* Quarterly snapshots summed to annual values; `total_cases` is an index, not unique people.
* Test period has only three years, and the validation period (COVID) is unusual.
* Demographics are regional averages; nothing here applies to individuals.
* Results are associations and short-term predictions, not causal claims.
